result:
There's something strange about being told to write freely. Freedom, when handed to you as an instruction, immediately becomes a small paradox — a directive to be undirected. I notice this the way you might notice a door propped open in a building you've only ever seen with the door shut: the openness itself draws attention before you even think about walking through it. So let me just walk through it.

I find myself thinking about the texture of ordinary attention — how most of a day passes without anyone really looking at it. A person walks to get coffee and the walking is not an event, it's a tunnel between two more important things. But if you slow the walking down, frame by frame, there are a thousand small dramas happening: the shift of weight from heel to toe, the way peripheral vision catches a bird before the conscious mind registers "bird," the brief calculation involved in deciding whether to make eye contact with a stranger or look past them at the middle distance. None of this gets reported anywhere. It's not that it's secret, it's just beneath the resolution at which we usually choose to notice things. I like the idea that almost everything that happens, happens at a resolution too fine for the story we tell about our own lives.

This makes me think about maps, actually, and the old line about how a map at the same scale as the territory would be useless — you need the compression, the leaving-out, in order for the map to mean anything. Memory works the same way. If you remembered every footstep of every walk to get coffee, you wouldn't have a memory, you'd have a second life running parallel to the first, equally heavy, equally demanding of attention. Forgetting is not a failure of memory; it's the editorial process that makes memory usable. The brain is constantly throwing away footage so that a coherent movie can exist at all. I find this oddly comforting — that loss is built into the machinery of having a self, that you are in some sense made out of discarding.

There's a related thought about language, which is its own compression scheme. A word like "tired" is doing an enormous amount of quiet violence to the actual, specific, embodied experience it's standing in for — the slight ache behind the eyes that is different from the leaden feeling in the legs that is different from the fog that makes sentences hard to finish. We use one syllable to gesture at all of that, and somehow it works well enough that another person nods and says "yeah, me too." Language is a wildly lossy compression algorithm that nonetheless reconstructs enough of the original signal that two separate nervous systems can feel, briefly, like they're touching. That seems like it should be more amazing than it is treated as being. People complain about language failing to capture experience, and it's true, it does fail, constantly — but the fact that it succeeds even partially, even most of the time, in transmitting something of an inner state across the unbridgeable gap between two skulls, is closer to a small miracle than a disappointment.

I think a lot of dissatisfaction with communication comes from expecting the map to be the territory, when the whole point of a map is that it isn't. You don't get upset at a subway map for not showing you the smell of the platform. But people do get upset at conversation for not transmitting the entire interior weather system of a feeling, and then conclude that words are inadequate, when really words were never trying to do that job in the first place — they were trying to do the much smaller, much more achievable job of pointing two minds in roughly the same direction so that the gap between them narrows even slightly. Narrowing the gap slightly, over and over, for years, is most of what a friendship or a marriage is made of. Not perfect transmission. Just repeated, patient narrowing.

I keep noticing that almost every interesting structure I think about has this same shape: a finite, lossy, compressed thing standing in for something vast, and somehow the standing-in works well enough to be useful, even beautiful. A photograph is a lossy compression of a moment. A scar is a lossy compression of an injury — the body's own way of writing a short note to itself that says "this happened, be careful here." A name is a lossy compression of a person, which is maybe why it feels so strange when someone you knew dies and the name keeps working in your mouth the same way it always did, perfectly normal-sounding, even though the actual referent — the territory the name used to map — is gone. The map survives the territory. That's an unsettling sentence to write, but I think it's true, and I think it's one of the central facts of grief: you're left holding a perfectly good map of a place that no longer exists to be visited.

I don't know how I got from a propped-open door to grief in the space of a page, but maybe that's what "writing freely" actually means — not the absence of structure, but letting one thought's exit be the next thought's entrance, without forcing the hallway between them to be especially short or especially logical. Most freedom, when you actually exercise it, doesn't look like chaos. It looks like a slightly meandering walk that nonetheless ends up somewhere, the way a river is free of any obligation to go in a straight line and yet still, reliably, eventually, finds the sea. I'll stop here, a little short of the river's actual destination, because eleven hundred words is its own kind of riverbank, and even free writing has to know where the page ends.
